title: Rate Limiter
oneLine: Enforce a policy close to the edge with atomic counters, bounded state, layered limits, and an explicit fail-open/fail-closed decision.
opening: I would place a coarse limiter at the gateway for DDoS and tenant protection, and optionally a finer limiter inside the service for business operations. My default algorithm is token bucket because it supports controlled bursts while enforcing a long-term rate. Rules are versioned and cached locally; shared usage state lives in a low-latency store such as Redis, updated atomically with Lua. The key can combine tenant, user, endpoint, IP, or API key, depending on the threat and fairness model. I would return 429 with retry metadata, emit decision telemetry, and decide per endpoint whether a limiter outage should fail open, fail closed, or fall back to conservative local quotas.
ask: What is being limited: user, tenant, IP, token, endpoint, cost unit, or a combination?
Are short bursts allowed, and what fairness guarantee is required?
Is the limiter global across regions or regional?
What should happen if the limiter store is unavailable?
scale: Estimate checks per second, not just accepted requests; rejected attacks may dominate.
State cardinality = active keys × windows/buckets; use TTL to bound it.
A global exact limiter adds cross-region latency—often regional allocation plus a global budget is the better trade-off.

decisions.default: Token bucket for most APIs; sliding-window counter when boundary fairness matters more.
decisions.why: Token bucket is compact, fast, and naturally supports controlled bursts.
decisions.switch: Leaky bucket for a fixed output rate; exact sliding log only for small cardinality/high-value limits.

decisions.default: Layer edge, gateway, and domain-specific limits.
decisions.why: Each layer protects a different scarce resource and avoids sending obvious abuse deeper.
decisions.switch: A library/sidecar may be appropriate when gateways cannot express business cost units.

decisions.default: Allocate regional budgets with periodic global reconciliation.
decisions.why: This preserves low latency and availability while bounding global overrun.
decisions.switch: Use a globally coordinated store for high-value operations where exceeding the quota is unacceptable.

decisions.default: Fail open for low-risk reads; fail closed or conservative-local for money movement, authentication, and abuse-sensitive writes.
decisions.why: The cost of denial versus excess traffic differs by endpoint.
decisions.switch: Use an emergency bypass with strict audit for operational recovery.

deepDives.title: Atomic token bucket
points: Store token count and last-refill timestamp in one key.
A Lua script computes refill, checks cost, decrements, and updates TTL atomically.
Use server time or monotonic semantics to reduce clock skew issues.

deepDives.title: Hierarchical limits
points: Check system capacity, tenant quota, user quota, and endpoint cost in a deterministic order.
Reject early on the cheapest check.
Expose which policy denied the request without leaking sensitive abuse signals.

deepDives.title: Client behavior
points: Return 429 and Retry-After or reset time.
Use jittered exponential backoff; do not encourage synchronized retries.
Offer quota headers carefully because exact remaining counts can be expensive or security-sensitive.

failures.response: Use a single atomic script/transaction; do not GET then SET in separate calls.

failures.risk: Hot tenant saturates one Redis shard
failures.response: Use local pre-allocation, shard large tenants by sub-key, or dedicate capacity while maintaining a global cap.
Use token bucket or sliding-window counter; test traffic at window edges.
Per-route fallback policy, local emergency buckets, circuit breaker, and auditable override.

questions.a: Token bucket limits the long-term rate while permitting a configured burst. Leaky bucket shapes output at a steady drain rate, which is useful when the downstream cannot absorb bursts.

questions.q: How do you rate-limit a request with variable cost?
questions.a: Charge tokens based on estimated work—rows scanned, model tokens, bytes, or operation class. Keep the cost function stable and versioned so clients and operators can reason about it.

questions.q: Can the limiter be perfectly global and highly available?
questions.a: Not without paying coordination latency or accepting bounded inconsistency during partitions. I would quantify tolerated overrun and choose regional budgets or a strongly consistent global path accordingly.

questions.q: How do you roll out new rules safely?
questions.a: Version policies, dry-run them first, compare would-block metrics, canary by tenant, then enforce. Keep instant rollback and audit history.

mistakes: Rate-limiting only by IP behind NAT or proxies
Saying fail open or closed globally instead of per route
seniorSignal: Treat rate limiting as a policy control plane plus a low-latency data plane. Discuss fairness, bounded inconsistency, rollout, and endpoint-specific failure behavior.
implementation: Redis Cluster + Lua script or a purpose-built limiter service
Spring Cloud Gateway/Envoy filters for edge enforcement
OpenTelemetry counters for allowed, blocked, fallback, and store latency
Policy version pushed through a config stream and cached locally
